claims.claim_text: A venture fund is a partnership between limited partners, who supply the money and hold very little control, and general partners, who supply very little of the money and hold most of the control; the trade for that asymmetry is that most of the financial upside returns to the limited partners.
claims.quote_verbatim: the limited partner puts in all the money and has very little control
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Venture capital began as wealthy individuals investing their own money, with no management fee because there was nothing to charge; the modern structure, in which a firm invests other people's money and its partners contribute perhaps one to five percent of the fund themselves, is now the overwhelming majority.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the way venture got started was, uh, was I'm going to take a bunch of my money
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Raising a first fund can be easier from individuals than from institutions: a partner at an established firm may write a personal cheque where the firm would not, and the mechanics of management fees make institutional money less attractive to a new manager in any case.
claims.quote_verbatim: You actually, uh, in many cases don't want to raise money from, uh, funds
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A venture fund's own business model sets the filter it applies: the lens is a company reaching roughly a hundred million dollars of revenue within about five to seven years, and the commonest reason for declining an otherwise good company and product is that it will not produce that scale in that time.
claims.quote_verbatim: what the industry will call venture returns, uh, which are big businesses, uh, doing, you know, typically in some number of years, five to seven years doing, you know, a hundred million dollars of revenue or more
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Seed-stage cheques from a hardware-focused fund run from around one hundred to one hundred and fifty thousand dollars at the low end up to five hundred or seven hundred and fifty thousand, scaled to the company's progress and the partners' confidence in the founders.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll write a, you know, a hundred or $150,000 check
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A five-hundred-thousand-dollar seed cheque is large to write and small relative to what building a business costs; companies that raised comparable sums through crowdfunding have failed for exactly that reason.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll write 500K checks, which is a lot. But at the same time, it's not very much in the grand scheme of getting a business built
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: The limited partners' requirement shapes how investors treat a portfolio company: a business that is somewhat profitable but never explosive is unwanted, so companies are pushed toward high-risk moves that either succeed or fail quickly and clear the books, on the arithmetic that one hit in five or ten returns the fund.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want what they call a lifestyle company in, uh, in their portfolio
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: The portfolio arithmetic is dominated by total losses: a fund's dozen large winners sit alongside thousands of investments that returned nothing at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: they got a dozen huge winners, but there's literally thousands they invested in that flopped and lost a hundred percent of their money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Almighty Dollarydoo

claims.claim_text: Investors hold preferred shares while founders and employees hold common stock, so in a wind-up or a sale the investors are repaid first; a founder's nominal percentage says little about what they receive.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have a higher priority in the stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Nerd Calendar

claims.claim_text: The preference is not theoretical: a company sold for one and a half million dollars against at least twenty million invested returns the proceeds to the investors before anyone else sees them.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they get paid back first
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: Raising more capital than the business needs is itself a failure mode: a company with a hundred million dollars of revenue can still collapse, because the obligation created by the money is to reach the investors' target rather than to be profitable.
claims.quote_verbatim: Tons of companies have taken too much investment capital
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motivational Speaker

claims.claim_text: Once a company has taken venture money it cannot simply be operated as a profitable business at its existing size, because the investors' return expectation is a multiple of what they put in.
claims.quote_verbatim: Once they took their venture capital money, they couldn't just operate it as
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Voltnuts for Flashlights

claims.claim_text: Accepting venture funding transfers control of direction: after that the founder either goes along with the direction the board sets or leaves the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you do that, you don't make the decisions anymore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Nadya Peek - Gallant Gcode Gerontology

claims.claim_text: Investors will apply pressure toward the outcome they need, and a recognised pattern is funding a company just short of what it requires, so that the final tranche is negotiated when the founders are desperate and costs a large additional share.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of times to give you just enough to get you on the edge of success
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Venture investors are not distinguished by temperament: the model is investing in risky ventures and requiring a large return in proportion to that risk, which is what governs their behaviour regardless of the individuals.
claims.quote_verbatim: they invest in risky stuff and they expect a large return for that large amount of risk
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: The expectation attached to investment reaches the working arrangements quickly: a research group folded into a venture-funded consulting firm on the understanding that it would keep operating as it had was questioned within a month or two about what its people were doing and what the exit strategy was.
claims.quote_verbatim: the VC said, wait a second, we want our money. What are, what are these seven guys doing?
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe Grand - Pancyclopaedic Prototyping Polymath

claims.claim_text: The unwritten terms attached to funding matter as much as the money: taking it implies raising a larger round the following year and selling or listing within about five years. An instrument that can be bought out, such as a convertible note, removes that obligation and lets a company be run for profit instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: the unwritten promise when you take any funding is like, you're going to go raise a bigger round next year
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Even a light investor relationship imposes useful discipline: quarterly requests for financials mean the company must actually keep them, which brings a bookkeeper, an accountant, and real profit and cash-flow statements.
claims.quote_verbatim: every quarter they email me and ask for the financials, um, which means I have to have financials
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Financing decisions are made against uncertainty about timing: a company took a further venture investment that in hindsight it did not need, because of the lag between finishing the product and the sales arriving.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had to take another venture investment, which we probably didn't need
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: A tool vendor's funding structure is a purchasing consideration for its customers, because no exit is good for them: a listing pushes the vendor toward growth and revenue extraction, and an acquisition usually ends in the product being shut down or absorbed.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're dealing with a VC funded company, there is no outcome that is good for you as a customer
claims.speaker: Jan Rychter
claims.episode_title: Component Management with Jan Rychter

claims.claim_text: Bootstrapping means starting with an amount of one's own money one can afford to lose, selling a small batch, and reinvesting the profit into a larger one. The failure rate of that path is very low where the failure rate of venture-funded ventures is high, because nothing is staked beyond what the founder can absorb.
claims.quote_verbatim: the failure rate there is huge, but the failure rate for bootstrapping is very, very low
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: Retaining ownership retains control: the majority shareholder decides, and a founder diluted to a few percent answers to shareholders on questions the founder used to settle. Putting in one's own money also aligns the effort, since the founder carries all of the risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more you hold onto the, the more control you have
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: A bootstrapped instrument company started with roughly a thousand dollars to build ten units, sold them, and compounded the profit into the next batch, with the internet supplying the distribution that would otherwise have needed a channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: You put in a thousand bucks to buy, to build 10 widgets, right? And then you sell them and make a profit and then you snowball that.
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Bootstrapping has become unusual enough that building a thirty-three-million-dollar business without outside funding is reported as remarkable, and graduates commonly believe that a funding round or a crowdfunding campaign is the only way to start a company.
claims.quote_verbatim: how one woman turned her passion for tinkering into a $33 million business without a dime of funding
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: The distribution of company formation is a power law whose visible tail is young founders, but the bulk of companies and of the revenue they generate comes from established engineers and business people; a startup does not have to mean a venture-funded attempt at a billion-dollar outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: a startup doesn't mean that you have to get venture capital funded and turn into a billion-dollar business or flop
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Aggravating Agersia Agiotage

claims.claim_text: Some businesses cannot be bootstrapped: a design tool built by an average of seven people over three years with effectively no sales represents about a million dollars of payroll before any revenue, which founders cannot self-fund, and working on it part-time means being overtaken.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're at a million dollars paid up front for a thing that doesn't make any money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Capital efficiency is achievable even in that model: one design-tool company raised about four hundred and fifty thousand dollars through an accelerator and a demo day, took roughly six hundred and fifty thousand in total, and ran on it for three years before raising a priced seed round.
claims.quote_verbatim: we got three years out of $650,000
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Deferring outside money is possible even in silicon: a fabless semiconductor company was founded with about eight or nine employees on the founders' own money, much of it from a previous acquisition, and operated for its first few years before taking venture funding from two firms.
claims.quote_verbatim: we managed without VC money for the first few years
claims.speaker: Oyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: The reason to delay a raise is price rather than independence: the same sum of money buys a smaller share of a company that has already been built up — ten percent rather than fifty.
claims.quote_verbatim: They'll get 10% instead of 50%
claims.speaker: Oyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: A lifestyle business is used as a disparaging term but describes a deliberate choice; the trade being made is a larger possible outcome against the conditions of one's own working life.
claims.quote_verbatim: People use lifestyle, uh, business as like a disparaging term
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: The Internet of Septage (with Akiba)

claims.claim_text: Venture capital began in the 1960s funding hardware — Fairchild and Intel — but modern practice runs against it: given a software and a hardware investment with comparable expected returns, an investor takes the software one, because hardware carries capital requirements and demands eight to ten distinct disciplines among the first fifteen employees.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the first 15 employees, you often can represent eight, nine, 10 distinct disciplines
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The standard rule for consumer hardware is that the selling price must be about four times the bill of materials for the business arithmetic to work, a multiple founders routinely find implausible until they run the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need a hardware company in the consumer space to carry a Forex, you know, multiple on their bomb in terms of their selling price just for the math to work
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Consumer hardware in particular is avoided because the ratio of failures to successes is so heavily skewed toward failure that the occasional large acquisition does not compensate.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ratio of death to success is, is so far skewed to failure right now
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: Hardware sold at twenty to thirty points of gross margin is not by itself an attractive business, which is why hardware companies were relatively underfunded. What changed the assessment was the redefinition of hardware as the means of delivering software into a user's life away from a screen.
claims.quote_verbatim: selling a widget for, you know, 20, 30 points of, of, of gross margin dollars, uh, is, is really challenging as a business
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: The premium investors place on growth speed disadvantages hardware structurally: scaling a physical product from one unit to a million is a machine that has to be built and cannot be built quickly, so capital flows to businesses whose marginal cost is near zero.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's really hard to make a widget and grow that from one to a million
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Almighty Dollarydoo

claims.claim_text: Entering the medium-volume hardware market takes roughly two to ten million dollars, which in practice comes from venture investors, and those investors expect the intellectual property to be protected — a direct tension with releasing the design openly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need anywhere from, you know, two to probably more like 10 million of funding
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Capital attention, not technical merit, determines which manufacturing technologies are publicly discussed: 3D printing is better marketed than precision casting largely because venture money is going into one and not the other.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3d printing is better marketed than precision casting
claims.speaker: Spencer Wright
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: The formal difference between an angel investor and a venture firm is the size of the cheque; the practical difference is that angels tend to be more useful and venture firms write larger cheques, so the choice is between people who help and money that is sufficient.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the size of the checks they write. Angels tend to be more useful. VCs tend to write bigger checks.
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Angels invest for reasons beyond return and expect the portfolio rather than any one company to pay; venture investors are doing it only to make money. The distinction is between someone whose job is investing and someone whose hobby it is.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're working with somebody whose job is investing versus somebody whose hobby is investing
claims.speaker: Zach Homet
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: An entrepreneur in residence is paid and given an office and a firm's full network of contacts, on the understanding that they will start a company the firm finds interesting; the firm may or may not fund it in the end.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll pay you and you'll get an office. You'll get all their contacts inside of venture capital
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: The arrangement carries a hazard: if the sponsoring firm then declines to fund the company, other investors read the decision as a mark against it regardless of the actual reason, and the founders still have to run the ordinary fundraising circuit.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it ends up being kind of a black mark
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Firms use more than one selection model: some choose the people and trust the eventual idea to follow, which is the accelerator model, and others pick an area of interest and fund several companies attacking it.
claims.quote_verbatim: The other one is to look at specific areas of interest and fund various companies that are going after that specific area of interest
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: A hardware accelerator supplies more than money — in some cases a machine shop and dedicated staff working alongside the founders — because hardware lacks the network of experienced people that software accelerators can draw on.
claims.quote_verbatim: in some cases a machine shop with a dedicated staff
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: For an investor the accelerator format replaces a decision made on a pitch in a week or two with three to six months of observation: how the team functions under stress, how it overcomes obstacles and how it pivots, so that by demo day the investor knows both the team and the product's evolution.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have the course of three months or six months to really get to know the entrepreneurs
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: An accelerator's purpose is to bring a team to the point of being fundable, and what investors will fund is high volume or a path to a hundred-million-dollar business; that requirement is what makes a domestic-only hardware accelerator difficult, since the manufacturing engine to replicate the product at those volumes has to exist somewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of these accelerators are really looking at truly accelerating a team to a point where they'll be fundable
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Accelerator operators do not necessarily hold the capital themselves: they raise it from investors on the strength of their expertise, and those investors take a share and get first access to the companies coming through the programme.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually go out to investors that go out they go out and they say we we have the knowledge
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: What an investor needs to hear is a believable plan to dominate a market; they knowingly discount a large share of it and still take the chance. Engineers who pitch too practically do badly at this, which is part of why implausible companies get funded.
claims.quote_verbatim: we believe half of what you're telling us is bullshit
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: A technically-run seed fund selects on the founders, and the ones that resonate arrive with half-disassembled prototypes wanting to discuss the algorithms running on the microcontroller rather than a polished pitch deck.
claims.quote_verbatim: people that come in with like business degrees and super polished pitch decks
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Some funds treat the investment as the start rather than the end of the work, advising and coaching the companies afterwards instead of acting only as cheque writers, and staff themselves with people who have built the kind of product they fund.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't see our, see ourselves as just like check writers
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: One seed thesis in this sector splits between the products themselves — low-cost robotics and connected devices — and the picks and shovels: the engineering, developer, manufacturing and prototyping tools used by everyone making products, with the fund entering as the first institutional money after the founders' own.
claims.quote_verbatim: Behind the scenes, we invest in picks and shovels
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Established industries with expensive problems and substantial revenue but no internal research and development are systematically underserved, because investors concentrated in one place tend to fund the problems they personally encounter and to look for a single outsized consumer success to cover the rest of the portfolio.
claims.quote_verbatim: people in Silicon Valley are a little too navel gazing
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Funding one's own problems is a specific selection failure: investors who are already wealthy will back wine services and private-jet programmes and thousand-dollar kitchen appliances, none of which address a problem an ordinary customer has.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they're only going to fund their own problems, they're only going to fund wine companies
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Investors commonly ask an open-source company about its patent position, but a founder who opens with their patents signals litigation rather than a business.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not here to fund a lawsuit
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: The first question from investors is often how many patents a company holds, so patents get filed to make the company presentable rather than because the founders wanted them.
claims.quote_verbatim: The first thing they ask you is how many patents you have
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: In semiconductors a patent portfolio is both defence and currency: a company of any size will eventually be sued whether or not it set out to infringe, so the size of the portfolio determines what it has to trade.
claims.quote_verbatim: the more portfolio patents you have, the more you have to trade
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: A failing company's patent portfolio has a second life: it is taken to an investor as a rescue, and the investor monetises it by asserting the patents against companies that are actually making things.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll go to a venture capital company with their patent portfolio and say, save us
claims.speaker: Jake Baker
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Investors who arrive after founding have no attachment to the conditions under which a company succeeded; their interest is the return, which is what puts an openly licensed product under pressure once the target is a company worth hundreds of millions rather than tens.
claims.quote_verbatim: they weren't the founders
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: The share-alike condition is the specific deterrent for investors, because building on the licensed work obliges the company to release its own work in turn.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's the thing that really scares the shit out of these venture capitalists
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: One open-source hardware company reached the conclusion after several years and its venture funding that it could not continue as a fully open company and grow into a major player in its industry, and closed several aspects of the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: we cannot continue as a 100% pure open source hardware company
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: The expectation of defensible intellectual property is a plausible contributor to the semiconductor industry's shift from open sharing to secrecy, since capital that funds a capital-intensive business wants to own what it funds.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want you to be open source, they want you to have defendable patents
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Venture funding is declinable: the developer of an open-source pick-and-place machine turned down an offer from one of the project's own backers rather than close the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: I told him to pound sand because I was not interested in like making it go close source
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: A crowdfunding campaign changes the negotiating position with investors: terms offered before the campaign demanded a large share, and once the campaign was visibly succeeding the same investors were calling to close, which let the company push back.
claims.quote_verbatim: even halfway through the Kickstarter campaign, we started getting phone calls and emails from these folks
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: One assessment at the time was that crowdfunding remained viable for hardware but not for software, except where the project was narrowly defined for a technical audience.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would not do a software project
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: An investor behind a crowdfunding campaign changes what the campaign can offer: instead of pricing at a hundred dollars against a fifty-dollar bill of materials at a five-hundred-unit minimum order, the company can commit to ten times the order quantity and price at seventy-five, reaching a wider audience.
claims.quote_verbatim: you should get MOQs that are 10 times that size
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Most products sold in general retail were never venture backed, so the question to settle first is whether one wants a venture-backable business or a good business; the second is well served by a modest crowdfunding campaign, shipping it, and moving to the next product.
claims.quote_verbatim: are you sure you want to build a venture-backable business or do you just want to build a great business?
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Venture capital is fuel poured on a fire: a small fire can be built up over time with twigs and logs, but pouring jet fuel on a fire that cannot accommodate it does not help.
claims.quote_verbatim: Venture capital is fuel that goes on a fire
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: A market with two entrenched vendors is harder to enter than one with a single dominant player: in programmable logic the two leaders fight each other and a new entrant is crushed incidentally. Around twenty companies have declared an intention to enter, none has succeeded, and capital continues to go in.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got two gorillas and they're fighting with each other in the middle of the ring
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Capital requirements vary enormously by sector: an EDA startup can begin as two people with laptops writing code, and one argument put to that industry is that a ten-million-dollar business run at twenty percent profit — about the scale of a dry-cleaning franchise — is a perfectly good outcome.
claims.quote_verbatim: being a startup in EDA could mean as little as a couple of guys getting together with their laptops to write some code
claims.speaker: Steve Leibson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Steve Leibson - Impavid Ideopraxist Insider

claims.claim_text: A company built on a technology from a doctoral thesis and funded by investors is under pressure toward an early sale rather than toward becoming a durable vendor, because the return has to be realised.
claims.quote_verbatim: The venture capitalists are the ones who gave you the money and they want to make their return
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Critical Mass

claims.claim_text: Funding history bounds an eventual sale price: roughly fifty million dollars of venture capital into a well-known board vendor implies it will not be sold for much under two hundred million, while its actual business — about two million boards a year with roughly eighty percent of income from hardware — does not obviously support that.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was $50 million venture capital that went into Arduino
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Welding with an HDMI Cable

claims.claim_text: Raising money is slow even for an operating company: a semiconductor firm losing money at a time when venture capital was hard to obtain took about nine months to raise against a written business plan, during which its chief executive did not know from one fortnight to the next whether payroll would clear.
claims.quote_verbatim: Took me about nine months to raise money
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: Engineers starting a company should be honest about what they are not good at and bring in a business person early to set the company up, handle the legal work, find the market and raise the money, which is itself high-value full-time work.
claims.quote_verbatim: you always need a very good business person to help you set the company up
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A startup career is less unstable than it appears from outside: once a company is funded, its board has a vested interest in its success, and a team that delivers, or at least delivers on enough and pivots sensibly, can generally raise the following round.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you get that first slug of venture capital and you fill your board with people who have a vested interest in your success
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: Some problems are funded outside the venture model entirely, by a wealthy individual who prefers difficult problems that take years and would not otherwise be backed.
claims.quote_verbatim: he just likes taking on really nasty problems that wouldn't normally be funded by venture capital
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies
